title: Exterior Photocontrols & Twist-Lock Receptacles

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Parking lot, demo area light head on a work table at ground level; box of photocontrols and caps. Medium shot.
scenes.says: Before you troubleshoot any exterior lighting, you need to know how the site is controlled. Individual photocontrols, a contactor and time clock, or a networked system. Get that wrong and you'll chase the wrong problem from a bucket 30 feet up. So plan it: find the control scheme before you climb, and bring the right caps and photocontrols for that voltage.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Graphic table beside the demo head.
scenes.on_screen: Photocontrol on each head = energized 24/7 | Shorting caps = contactor control, dead in daytime
scenes.says: How to tell. A twist-lock photocontrol on top of each head means the circuit is energized 24/7 and each fixture switches itself. Shorting caps, or no receptacle, mean a contactor at the building switches the circuit, and it's dead in daytime. A 7-pin receptacle with a node means a networked system. And a wall pack may have a small button photocell built in.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up: 3-pin and 7-pin receptacles side by side; graphic labels Line, Load, Neutral, pins 4-5, pins 6-7.
scenes.says: The receptacle. ANSI C136.10 is the standard 3-pin: line, typically black, load, typically red, and neutral, typically white. On 480-volt systems that third pin may be a second line conductor, so read the label. ANSI C136.41 adds pins for 0 to 10 volt dimming and signals, making 5-pin or 7-pin receptacles. They still accept 3-pin photocontrols.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up: trainer rotates the receptacle so the photocontrol window faces north, then twists in a photocontrol; then removes it and installs a shorting cap.
scenes.on_screen: Window faces NORTH. Shorting cap = always on when energized.
scenes.says: Most receptacles rotate. Point the photocontrol window north, away from direct sun. Now caps. A shorting cap connects line to load, so the fixture is on whenever the circuit is energized. It's only for contactor or time clock control. A non-shorting cap seals the receptacle and keeps the fixture off.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew beside the demo head, medium close-up.
scenes.on_screen: Individual photocontrol site + shorting cap = burns 24/7. Match the voltage rating.
scenes.says: The common mix-up: on a site with individual photocontrols, someone installs a shorting cap and that fixture burns 24/7. Half the lot on all day? Look for shorting caps on a 24/7 circuit, or a contactor in HAND. And match the voltage. A 120-volt-only photocontrol on a 277-volt fixture fails immediately. Many utility-style photocontrols fail on, so one day-burner often means a failed-on photocontrol.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up: trainer covers the photocontrol with an opaque test cap; on-screen timer counts the delay; fixture lights.
scenes.on_screen: 1 Inspect  2 Cover test, wait the delay  3 Swap test or shorting cap  4 Night: is the circuit energized?
scenes.says: Testing. Inspect for damage and water. In daytime, cover the sensor window completely with an opaque cap and wait through the turn-on delay, seconds to a couple of minutes. It should light. No? Swap in a known-good photocontrol or a temporary shorting cap. If it lights now, the photocontrol is the problem. If not, it's the receptacle, wiring, fuse, driver or circuit.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: At dusk, a fixture cycling on and off next to a lit sign.
scenes.on_screen: Cycling at dusk = photocontrol seeing other light. Re-orient or shield.
scenes.says: Cycling at dusk usually means the photocontrol is reading light from a neighbor fixture, a lit sign or a reflective wall. Re-orient the receptacle, or use a photocontrol with a different turn-off ratio, or a shield.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Trainer in a bucket at a pole head; then at the panel applying a lock.
scenes.on_screen: Receptacle terminals = line voltage. Don't reach in. LOTO before opening the head.
scenes.says: Safety. Twist-lock receptacles are at line voltage, often 277 or 480, and usually reached from a MEWP. Swapping a photocontrol is routine, but the terminals are exposed when it's off. Don't reach into the receptacle or the head. Before opening the luminaire, rewiring a receptacle or replacing a driver, lock out at the panel and verify absence of voltage at the luminaire.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.on_screen: Now read the lesson and take the quiz.
scenes.says: To replace a receptacle: lock out, verify, note the wire positions, use the same pin count and rating, keep the gasket, rotate north, and install the right photocontrol or cap. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Demo head on a ground-level table, energized only via a qualified setup for the cover test. Generic unbranded photocontrols and caps. Senior tech performs demonstrations; presenter voice-over in scenes 4, 6.
